approved: Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Competition and Consumer) Bill 2019
Communications, Cyber Safety and the Arts
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would put in place the main parts of the government's plan for broadband regulation, based on a 2014 review.

It would change the rules for superfast fixed-line networks to make the default separation requirement clearer and let the competition regulator approve functional separation or exempt small new networks.
Non-discrimination rules would apply to eligible services on lines built three months after the bill becomes law.
Reset the structural separation arrangements for superfast networks.
Establish functional separation as an option approved by the ACCC.
Let the ACCC exempt small start-up networks from separation rules.
Remove regulation of networks that serve small business customers.
Grandfather existing wholesale-only obligations for networks built between 1 January 2011 and the designated commencement date.
Let the Minister extend existing exemptions but not grant new ones after the designated commencement date.
Operators of superfast fixed-line networks, access seekers, and the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission.

The majority voted against an [amendment](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debates/?id=2020-02-13.25.2) to the usual [second reading](https://www.peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/) motion, which is that the majority agree to read the bill for a second time (parliamentary jargon for agreeing with the main idea of the bill). This means the amendment failed. ### Amendment text > *That all words after "That" be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:* > > *"whilst not declining to give the bill a second reading, the House:* > > *(1) notes that:* > >> *(a) evidence provided to the Senate indicates that NBN Co reduced regional investment by $200 million between 2018 and 2022 relative to the 2019 Corporate Plan;* >> >> *(b) this decrease in regional investment was concealed in the 2020 NBN Co Corporate Plan; and* >> >> *(c) NBN Co has given three contradictory and unsatisfactory explanations as to why investment in regional networks was reduced;* > > *(2) further notes significant concerns that the Government is introducing a broadband tax in the name of regional funding, while reducing regional investment in broadband networks in the NBN 2020 Corporate Plan; and* > > *(3) calls on the Government to restore the funding allocation for investment in regional NBN networks".*

The bill was reintroduced to improve superfast broadband provision, with measures including relaxed carrier separation rules allowing non‑NBN Co carriers to operate wholesale and retail, new statutory obligations on NBN Co to connect premises at minimum 25/5 Mbps speeds and cover 92% of premises, and a Regional Broadband Scheme funded by a $7.10 monthly charge per premises on high‑speed fixed‑line carriers. The bills also incorporate opposition amendments and require a review within four years.

The bill establishes a monthly charge of $7.09 (base component) with a $7.10 combined cap (both indexed) on carriers per active fixed-line superfast broadband connection from 1 July 2020, to fund NBN Co's fixed-wireless and satellite network losses and replace its internal cross-subsidy, with the administrative cost component funding the Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) and the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC). The scheme ensures all NBN-comparable fixed-line networks contribute transparently to regional broadband, supporting up to one million premises mostly in remote areas, after minor changes were made in line with opposition proposals.

Labor supported the bill but criticised the government for reducing regional NBN investment by $200 million between 2018 and 2022, concealed in the 2020 Corporate Plan, while introducing a broadband tax; it called for restored regional funding and independent, transparent modelling of the levy.

Labor supported the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Competition and Consumer) Bill 2019 to establish a statutory infrastructure provider regime ensuring universal high-speed broadband access, but criticised the Coalition's multitechnology mix NBN approach for costing $200 million more per year to maintain and reducing revenue by $300 million, while Australia's internet speed ranking fell from 50th to 68th globally. The Telecommunications (Regional Broadband Scheme) Charge Bill 2019 imposes a new $7.10 per month broadband tax on households and businesses connected to non-NBN networks, which Labor will allow to pass but will address concerns in the Senate.

The speaker argued that the government's changes to the NBN have widened the digital divide, particularly in regional Australia, and criticised the $7 per month broadband levy as a tax on consumers. They supported the bill but highlighted failures including a $200 million cut to fixed wireless, Australia's drop to 68th in global internet speeds, and the NBN being four years behind schedule and $20 billion over budget.

The speaker argued that the Morrison government's NBN rollout has been a dismal failure, with costs blowing out to $51 billion and the project running four years behind schedule, while also criticising the government's handling of the NDIS. They listed 12 specific consumer issues with NBN services, including poor technical support, high prices, and inadequate service reliability, and noted Australia ranked fourth slowest in the OECD for broadband speeds.

The government's telecommunications reform package includes revised carrier separation rules, statutory infrastructure provider obligations for NBN Co, and a Regional Broadband Scheme funded by a $7.10 per-month-per-premises charge on fixed-line carriers to support regional satellite and fixed-wireless services. The reforms set minimum peak speeds of 25 Mbps download and 5 Mbps upload, with the NBN projected to boost GDP by $10.4 billion annually.
